claim: 17.7% of all CDKN2A missense variants were functionally deleterious.
source: We found that 17.7% of all missense variants were functionally deleterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput functional assay described in the manuscript.

claim: All in silico models performed similarly when compared to functional classifications with accuracies of 39.5–85.4%.
source: Notably, we found that all in silico models performed similarly when compared to our functional classifications with accuracies of 39.5–85.4%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing in silico predictions to functional assay results.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched within ankyrin repeats.
source: Furthermore, while we found that functionally deleterious variants were enriched within ankyrin repeats, we did not identify any residues where all missense variants were functionally deleterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing distribution of functionally deleterious variants across protein domains.

claim: No residues were identified where all missense variants were functionally deleterious.
source: Furthermore, while we found that functionally deleterious variants were enriched within ankyrin repeats, we did not identify any residues where all missense variants were functionally deleterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data examining all possible missense variants at each residue.

claim: Genetic testing of patients with cancer to identify variants associated with increased cancer risk is becoming more common.
source: Genetic testing of patients with cancer to identify variants associated with an increased cancer risk and sensitivity to targeted therapies is becoming more common as broad testing criteria are integrated into clinical care guidelines (Goggins et al., 2020; Stoffel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical care guidelines.

claim: The American College of Medical Genetics provides a framework to integrate multiple types of evidence for variant interpretation.
source: The American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) provides a framework to integrate multiple types of evidence, including variant characteristics, disease epidemiology, clinical information, and functional classifications, to interpret variants in any gene (Richards et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the ACMG guidelines publication.

claim: In silico variant effect predictors are integrated into ACMG variant interpretation guidelines as supporting evidence.
source: In silico variant effect predictors are also integrated into ACMG variant interpretation guidelines as supporting evidence to aid classification of variants.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of ACMG guidelines.

claim: Varied accuracy, poor agreement between models, and inflated performance on publicly available data have been reported for in silico variant effect predictors.
source: While numerous models have been developed, varied accuracy, poor agreement between models, and inflated performance on publicly available data have been reported (Cubuk et al., 2021; Jaffe et al., 2011; Wilcox et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies evaluating in silico predictors.

claim: Recently developed variant effect predictors aim to overcome limitations by incorporating deep-learning-based protein structure predictions and by not training on human annotated datasets.
source: Recently developed variant effect predictors aim to overcome these limitations by incorporating deep-learning-based protein structure predictions and by not training on human annotated datasets (Brandes et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent publications on machine learning-based predictors.

claim: Post-development assessment of machine learning-based variant effect predictors to determine accuracy on novel experimental datasets and suitability for clinical use are limited.
source: However, post-development assessment of machine learning-based variant effect predictors, to determine accuracy on novel experimental datasets and suitability for clinical use, are limited.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature review and establishes the gap this study addresses.

claim: Germline VUSs in hereditary cancer genes are a common finding in patients with cancer.
source: Germline VUSs in hereditary cancer genes are a common finding in patients with cancer and frequently can be reclassified as pathogenic on the basis of in vitro functional evidence (Kimura et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Germline CDKN2A VUSs are found in up to 4.3% of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
source: In patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), germline CDKN2A VUSs affecting p16INK4a, most often rare missense variants, are found in up to 4.3% of patients (Chaffee et al., 2018; Kimura et al., 2021; McWilliams et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Shindo et al., 2017; Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Over 40% of CDKN2A VUSs assayed in a previous study were functionally deleterious and could be reclassified as likely pathogenic.
source: We found that over 40% of VUSs assayed were functionally deleterious and could reclassified as likely pathogenic.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Expression of codon-optimized CDKN2A in PANC-1 cells resulted in significant reduction in cell proliferation (p-value<0.0001).
source: Expression of codon-optimized CDKN2A or the synonymous CDKN2A variants, p.L32L, p.G101G, and p.V126V, in PANC-1, a PDAC cell line with a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A, resulted in significant reduction in cell proliferation (p-value<0.0001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no significant difference between codon-optimized CDKN2A and three synonymous variants assayed in cell proliferation.
source: There was no significant difference between codon-optimized CDKN2A and the three synonymous variants assayed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell proliferation assays.

claim: Expression of three pathogenic variants (p.L32P, p.G101W, and p.V126D) in PANC-1 cells did not result in any significant changes in cell proliferation.
source: Conversely, expression of three pathogenic variants, p.L32P, p.G101W, and p.V126D, in PANC-1 cells did not result in any significant changes in cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell proliferation assays.

claim: No statistically significant changes in barcode representation were found in the CellTag library assay, indicating that representation of functionally neutral variants is stable over the assay time course.
source: We found no statistically significant changes in barcode representation, indicating that representation of a pool of functionally neutral variants is stable over a period of in vitro culture representing our assay time course (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 27 variants (0.87% of 3120) were represented in the plasmid libraries at ≤1%.
source: Twenty-seven variants (27 of 3120, 0.87%) were represented in the plasmid libraries at ≤1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from plasmid library characterization.

claim: The proportion of each variant in the amplified plasmid library and in the cell pool at day 9 were highly correlated.
source: The proportion of each variant in the amplified plasmid library and in the cell pool at day 9 were highly correlated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: CDKN2A variant p.V126D was previously reported as pathogenic and increased representation during in vitro proliferation.
source: CDKN2A variant p.V126D (*) was previously reported as pathogenic and increased representation during in vitro proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and previous literature.

claim: CDKN2A variant p.R144C was previously reported as benign variant and maintained representation during in vitro proliferation.
source: CDKN2A variant p.R144C (**) was previously reported as benign variant and maintained representation during in vitro proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and previous literature.

claim: 525 of 2964 missense variants (17.7%) were functionally deleterious in the assay.
source: We found that 525 of 2964 missense variants (17.7%) were functionally deleterious in our assay (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 1784 variants (60.2%) were classified as functionally neutral.
source: In addition, 1784 variants (60.2%) were classified as functionally neutral, with the remaining 655 variants (22.1%) classified as indeterminate function (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 655 variants (22.1%) were classified as indeterminate function.
source: In addition, 1784 variants (60.2%) were classified as functionally neutral, with the remaining 655 variants (22.1%) classified as indeterminate function (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 27 of 32 (84.4%) benchmark pathogenic variants were functionally deleterious in the assay.
source: Of variants identified in patients with cancer and previously reported to be functionally deleterious in published literature and/or reported in ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (benchmark pathogenic variants), 27 of 32 (84.4%) were functionally deleterious in our assay (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, Supplementary file 4; Chaffee et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2016; Horn et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2018; Kimura et al., 2022; McWilliams et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Zhen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous literature.

claim: All 156 synonymous variants and six missense variants previously reported as functionally neutral were characterized as functionally neutral in the assay.
source: Of 156 synonymous variants and six missense variants previously reported to be functionally neutral in published literature and/or reported in ClinVar as benign or likely benign (benchmark benign variants), all were characterized as functionally neutral in our assay (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, Supplementary file 4; Kimura et al., 2022; McWilliams et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous literature.

claim: 28 of 31 VUSs (90.3%) previously reported to be functionally deleterious were functionally deleterious in the assay.
source: Of 31 VUSs previously reported to be functionally deleterious, 28 (90.3%) were functionally deleterious and 3 (9.7%) were of indeterminate function in our assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing to previously reported VUSs.

claim: 16 of 18 VUSs (88.9%) previously reported to be functionally neutral were functionally neutral in the assay.
source: Similarly, of 18 VUSs previously reported to be functionally neutral, 16 (88.9%) were functionally neutral and 2 (11.1%) were of indeterminate function in our assay (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing to previously reported VUSs.

claim: 452 of 560 missense variants (80.7%) had the same functional classification in each of two replicates.
source: The majority of missense variants, 452 of 560 (80.7%), had the same functional classification in each of the two replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from duplicate assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No variant was functionally deleterious in one replicate and functionally neutral in another.
source: Importantly, no variant that was functionally deleterious in one replicate and functionally neutral in another (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from duplicate assays.

claim: 53 of 2964 missense variants (1.8%) were present in the cell pool at day 9 at <2%.
source: Fifty-three of 2964 missense variants (1.8%) were present in the cell pool at day 9 of the first assay replicate (experiment 1) at <2%, as determined by the number of sequence reads supporting the variant (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of variants classified as functionally deleterious for variants present in less than 2% versus more than 2% of the cell pool at day 9 (p-value=0.28).
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of variants classified as functionally deleterious for variants present in less than 2% of the cell pool at day 9 (12 of 53 variants; 22.6%), and variants present in more than 2% of the cell pool (496 of 2911 variants; 17.0%) (p-value=0.28) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Accuracy of in silico model predictions were 39.5–85.4% (CADD – 45.1%; PolyPhen-2 – 39.5%; SIFT – 60.9%; VEST – 71.9%; AlphaMissense – 71.6%; ESM1b – 59.2%; and PrimateAI-3D – 85.4%).
source: Accuracy of in silico model predictions were 39.5–85.4% (CADD – 45.1%; PolyPhen-2 – 39.5%; SIFT – 60.9%; VEST – 71.9%; AlphaMissense – 71.6%; ESM1b – 59.2%; and PrimateAI-3D – 85.4%) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of in silico predictions to experimental functional classifications shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sensitivity of in silico models was 0.25–0.98 (CADD – 0.97; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.79; VEST – 0.91; AlphaMissense – 0.94; ESM1b – 0.95; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.25).
source: We found that sensitivity was 0.25–0.98 (CADD – 0.97; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.79; VEST – 0.91; AlphaMissense – 0.94; ESM1b – 0.95; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.25), specificity was 0.27–0.98 (CADD – 0.35; PolyPhen-2 – 0.27; SIFT – 0.57; VEST – 0.68; AlphaMissense – 0.67; ESM1b – 0.51; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.98), positive predictive value was 0.22–0.68 (CADD – 0.23; PolyPhen-2 – 0.22; SIFT – 0.28; VEST – 0.38; AlphaMissense – 0.38; ESM1b – 0.3; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.68), and negative predictive value was 0.87–0.98 (CADD – 0.98; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.93; VEST – 0.97; AlphaMissense – 0.98; ESM1b – 0.98; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.87).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing in silico predictions to experimental data.

claim: Specificity of in silico models was 0.27–0.98 (CADD – 0.35; PolyPhen-2 – 0.27; SIFT – 0.57; VEST – 0.68; AlphaMissense – 0.67; ESM1b – 0.51; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.98).
source: We found that sensitivity was 0.25–0.98 (CADD – 0.97; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.79; VEST – 0.91; AlphaMissense – 0.94; ESM1b – 0.95; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.25), specificity was 0.27–0.98 (CADD – 0.35; PolyPhen-2 – 0.27; SIFT – 0.57; VEST – 0.68; AlphaMissense – 0.67; ESM1b – 0.51; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.98), positive predictive value was 0.22–0.68 (CADD – 0.23; PolyPhen-2 – 0.22; SIFT – 0.28; VEST – 0.38; AlphaMissense – 0.38; ESM1b – 0.3; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.68), and negative predictive value was 0.87–0.98 (CADD – 0.98; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.93; VEST – 0.97; AlphaMissense – 0.98; ESM1b – 0.98; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.87).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing in silico predictions to experimental data.

claim: Positive predictive value of in silico models was 0.22–0.68 (CADD – 0.23; PolyPhen-2 – 0.22; SIFT – 0.28; VEST – 0.38; AlphaMissense – 0.38; ESM1b – 0.3; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.68).
source: We found that sensitivity was 0.25–0.98 (CADD – 0.97; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.79; VEST – 0.91; AlphaMissense – 0.94; ESM1b – 0.95; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.25), specificity was 0.27–0.98 (CADD – 0.35; PolyPhen-2 – 0.27; SIFT – 0.57; VEST – 0.68; AlphaMissense – 0.67; ESM1b – 0.51; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.98), positive predictive value was 0.22–0.68 (CADD – 0.23; PolyPhen-2 – 0.22; SIFT – 0.28; VEST – 0.38; AlphaMissense – 0.38; ESM1b – 0.3; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.68), and negative predictive value was 0.87–0.98 (CADD – 0.98; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.93; VEST – 0.97; AlphaMissense – 0.98; ESM1b – 0.98; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.87).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing in silico predictions to experimental data.

claim: Negative predictive value of in silico models was 0.87–0.98 (CADD – 0.98; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.93; VEST – 0.97; AlphaMissense – 0.98; ESM1b – 0.98; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.87).
source: We found that sensitivity was 0.25–0.98 (CADD – 0.97; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.79; VEST – 0.91; AlphaMissense – 0.94; ESM1b – 0.95; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.25), specificity was 0.27–0.98 (CADD – 0.35; PolyPhen-2 – 0.27; SIFT – 0.57; VEST – 0.68; AlphaMissense – 0.67; ESM1b – 0.51; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.98), positive predictive value was 0.22–0.68 (CADD – 0.23; PolyPhen-2 – 0.22; SIFT – 0.28; VEST – 0.38; AlphaMissense – 0.38; ESM1b – 0.3; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.68), and negative predictive value was 0.87–0.98 (CADD – 0.98; PolyPhen-2 – 0.98; SIFT – 0.93; VEST – 0.97; AlphaMissense – 0.98; ESM1b – 0.98; and PrimateAI-3D – 0.87).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing in silico predictions to experimental data.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01).
source: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01), ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10), and ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11), while depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13) and non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10).
source: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01), ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10), and ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11), while depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13) and non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11).
source: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01), ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10), and ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11), while depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13) and non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13).
source: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01), ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10), and ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11), while depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13) and non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Functionally deleterious variants were depleted in non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0).
source: Functionally deleterious variants were enriched in ankyrin repeat 1 (21.0%, adjusted p-value=0.01), ankyrin repeat 2 (26.2%, adjusted p-value=1.0 × 10–10), and ankyrin repeat 3 (26.3%, adjusted p-value=2.6 × 10–11), while depleted in ankyrin repeat 4 (6.5%, adjusted p-value=3.2 × 10–13) and non-ankyrin repeat regions (6.8%, adjusted p-value=0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: 37.0% of variants in residues 16–25 of ankyrin repeat 1 were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: Moreover, functionally deleterious variants were further enriched within 10 residue subregions of ankyrin repeats 1–3, with 37.0% of variants in residues 16–25 of ankyrin repeat 1, 40.0% of variants in residues 46–55 of ankyrin repeat 2, and 48.0% of variants in residues 80–89 of ankyrin repeat 3 being classified as functionally deleterious (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 40.0% of variants in residues 46–55 of ankyrin repeat 2 were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: Moreover, functionally deleterious variants were further enriched within 10 residue subregions of ankyrin repeats 1–3, with 37.0% of variants in residues 16–25 of ankyrin repeat 1, 40.0% of variants in residues 46–55 of ankyrin repeat 2, and 48.0% of variants in residues 80–89 of ankyrin repeat 3 being classified as functionally deleterious (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 48.0% of variants in residues 80–89 of ankyrin repeat 3 were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: Moreover, functionally deleterious variants were further enriched within 10 residue subregions of ankyrin repeats 1–3, with 37.0% of variants in residues 16–25 of ankyrin repeat 1, 40.0% of variants in residues 46–55 of ankyrin repeat 2, and 48.0% of variants in residues 80–89 of ankyrin repeat 3 being classified as functionally deleterious (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mean percent of functionally deleterious missense variants across all single residues was 17.7% (95% confidence interval: 12.7–20.9%).
source: Across all single residues, the mean percent of functionally deleterious missense variants was 17.7% (95% confidence interval: 12.7–20.9%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claim: At five amino acid residues (p.G23, p.G55, p.H83, p.D84, and p.G89), 17 of 19 (89.5%) possible missense variants were functionally deleterious.
source: At five amino acid residues, p.G23, p.G55, p.H83, p.D84, and p.G89, 17 of 19 (89.5%) possible missense variants were functionally deleterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the functional assay.

claim: Residues p.G23, p.G55, p.H83, p.D84, and p.G89 are conserved between human and murine p16.
source: Notably, these residues are conserved between human and murine p16 (Byeon et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on protein conservation.

claim: p.H83 has been reported to stabilize peptide loops connecting the helix-turn-helix structure of the four ankyrin repeats.
source: And p.H83 has been reported to stabilize peptide loops connecting the helix-turn-helix structure of the four ankyrin repeats (Byeon et al., 1998), whereas p.D84 and p.G89 are located in a 20-residue region reported to interact with CDK4 and CDK6 (Fåhraeus et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published structural studies.

claim: p.D84 and p.G89 are located in a 20-residue region reported to interact with CDK4 and CDK6.
source: And p.H83 has been reported to stabilize peptide loops connecting the helix-turn-helix structure of the four ankyrin repeats (Byeon et al., 1998), whereas p.D84 and p.G89 are located in a 20-residue region reported to interact with CDK4 and CDK6 (Fåhraeus et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published functional studies.

claim: 18 residues were tolerant of amino acid substitutions, with no missense variant characterized as functionally deleterious.
source: Conversely, 18 residues were tolerant of amino acid substitutions, with no missense variant characterized as functionally deleterious in our assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claim: 355 unique missense somatic mutations were reported in COSMIC, TCGA, JHU, and MSK-IMPACT, of which 119 (33.5%) were functionally deleterious.
source: Overall, 355 unique missense somatic mutations were reported, of which 119 (33.5%) were functionally deleterious in our assay (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases.

claim: The percent of missense somatic mutations that were classified as functionally deleterious was greater than the percent of all possible CDKN2A missense variants classified as functionally deleterious, suggesting enrichment of functionally deleterious missense changes among somatic mutations.
source: The percent of missense somatic mutations that were classified as functionally deleterious was greater than the percent of all possible CDKN2A missense variants classified as functionally deleterious, suggesting enrichment of functionally deleterious missense changes among somatic mutations (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 4, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing somatic mutation data to all possible variants.

claim: 34.2–53.4% of unique missense somatic mutations were classified as functionally deleterious.
source: We found that 34.2–53.4% of unique missense somatic mutations classified as functionally deleterious, with 61.4–67.6% of patients having a functionally deleterious somatic mutation (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 61.4–67.6% of patients had a functionally deleterious somatic mutation.
source: We found that 34.2–53.4% of unique missense somatic mutations classified as functionally deleterious, with 61.4–67.6% of patients having a functionally deleterious somatic mutation (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 32.4–50.0% of all functionally deleterious missense somatic mutations occurred within ankyrin repeat 3.
source: We found that 32.4–50.0% of all functionally deleterious missense somatic mutations occurred within ankyrin repeat 3, with 48.0–58.0% of patients in each cohort having a functionally deleterious missense somatic mutation in this domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases.

claim: 48.0–58.0% of patients in each cohort had a functionally deleterious missense somatic mutation in ankyrin repeat 3.
source: We found that 32.4–50.0% of all functionally deleterious missense somatic mutations occurred within ankyrin repeat 3, with 48.0–58.0% of patients in each cohort having a functionally deleterious missense somatic mutation in this domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases.

claim: 65.7–76.0% of functionally deleterious missense somatic mutations in ankyrin repeat 3 were in residues 80–89.
source: Notably, 65.7–76.0% of functionally deleterious missense somatic mutations in this domain were in residues 80–89 (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data applied to somatic mutation databases.

claim: 26 of 355 (7.3%) unique missense somatic mutations would be classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic by ACMG classification guidelines.
source: When considering unique missense somatic mutations, 26 of 355 (7.3%) would be classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic by ACMG classification guidelines and these were found in 263 of 1176 (22.4%) patients in COSMIC, 45 of 185 (24.3%) patients in TCGA, 40 of 184 (21.7%) patients in JHU, and 46 of 174 (26.4%) patients in MSK-IMPACT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on applying ACMG guidelines to somatic mutation data.

claim: The most prevalent somatic mutations that could be classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic were p.His83Tyr and p.Asp84Asn.
source: In each cohort, the most prevalent of these somatic mutations were p.His83Tyr and p.Asp84Asn, with more than half of the patients with a somatic mutation that could be classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic having either the p.His83Tyr or p.Asp84Asn alteration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of somatic mutation databases shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a statistically significant depletion of functionally deleterious mutations in colorectal adenocarcinoma (20.4%; adjusted p-value=5.4 × 10–9).
source: When considering missense somatic mutation reported in any database, there was a statistically significant depletion of functionally deleterious mutations in colorectal adenocarcinoma (20.4%; adjusted p-value=5.4 × 10–9) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of somatic mutation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: gnomAD v4.1.0 reports 287 missense variants in CDKN2A, including 13 pathogenic, 4 likely pathogenic, 3 likely benign, 3 benign, and 264 VUSs.
source: The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) v4.1.0 reports 287 missense variants in CDKN2A, including the 13 pathogenic, 4 likely pathogenic, 3 likely benign, 3 benign, and 264 VUSs classified using ACMG variant interpretation guidelines (Figure 5A and B, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the gnomAD database.

claim: Of 264 missense VUSs in gnomAD, 177 (67.0%) were functionally neutral, 56 (21.2%) were indeterminate function, and 31 (11.7%) were functionally deleterious.
source: Of the 264 missense VUSs, 177 were functionally neutral (67.0%), 56 (21.2%) were indeterminate function, and 31 (11.7%) were functionally deleterious in our assay using the gamma GLM for classification (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by applying experimental functional classifications to gnomAD variants shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ClinVar reports 395 CDKN2A missense VUSs, of which 256 (64.8%) were functionally neutral, 94 (23.8%) were indeterminate function, and 45 (11.4%) were functionally deleterious.
source: Similarly, ClinVar reports 395 CDKN2A missense VUSs, of which 256 (64.8%) were functionally neutral, 94 (23.8%) were indeterminate function, and 45 (11.4%) were functionally deleterious in our assay (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by applying experimental functional classifications to ClinVar variants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The functional assay provides evidence to reclassify 301 of 395 (76.2%) missense VUSs reported in ClinVar.
source: Importantly, our functionally assay provides evidence to reclassify 301 of 395 (76.2%) missense VUSs reported in ClinVar and 208 of 264 (78.8%) missense VUSs reported in gnomAD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference that functional data can be used to reclassify VUSs according to ACMG guidelines.

claim: The functional assay provides evidence to reclassify 208 of 264 (78.8%) missense VUSs reported in gnomAD.
source: Importantly, our functionally assay provides evidence to reclassify 301 of 395 (76.2%) missense VUSs reported in ClinVar and 208 of 264 (78.8%) missense VUSs reported in gnomAD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference that functional data can be used to reclassify VUSs according to ACMG guidelines.

claim: 45 (11.4%) VUSs in ClinVar could be reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
source: These include 45 (11.4%) VUSs in ClinVar and 31 missense VUSs in gnomAD that could be reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference that functionally deleterious VUSs can be reclassified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines.

claim: 31 missense VUSs in gnomAD could be reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
source: These include 45 (11.4%) VUSs in ClinVar and 31 missense VUSs in gnomAD that could be reclassified as likely pathogenic variants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference that functionally deleterious VUSs can be reclassified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines.

claim: PANC-1 is a human PDAC cell line with a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A.
source: PANC-1 (American Type Culture Collection, Manassas, VA, USA; catalog no. CRL-1469), a human PDAC cell line with a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A (Caldas et al., 1994) and 293T (American Type Culture Collection; catalog no. CRL-3216), a human embryonic kidney cell line, were maintained in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc, Waltham, MA, USA; catalog no. 11995-065) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc; catalog no. 26140-079).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature characterizing the PANC-1 cell line.

claim: CDKN2A contains four ankyrin repeats: ankyrin repeat 1 at codon 11–40, ankyrin repeat 2 at codon 44–72, ankyrin repeat 3 at codon 77–106, and ankyrin repeat 4 at codon 110–139.
source: CDKN2A contains four ankyrin repeats that mediate protein-protein interactions, ankyrin repeat 1 at codon 11–40, ankyrin repeat 2 at codon 44–72, ankyrin repeat 3 at codon 77–106, and ankyrin repeat 4 at codon 110–139 (Goldstein, 2004; Ruas and Peters, 1998; Sun et al., 2010; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on CDKN2A structure.

claim: Ankyrin repeats mediate protein-protein interactions.
source: CDKN2A contains four ankyrin repeats that mediate protein-protein interactions, ankyrin repeat 1 at codon 11–40, ankyrin repeat 2 at codon 44–72, ankyrin repeat 3 at codon 77–106, and ankyrin repeat 4 at codon 110–139 (Goldstein, 2004; Ruas and Peters, 1998; Sun et al., 2010; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on ankyrin repeat function.

claim: 517 of 525 variants (98.5%) classified as functionally deleterious using the gamma GLM were similarly classified using log2 normalized fold change.
source: Notably, 517 of 525 variants (98.5%) classified as functionally deleterious and 1586 of 1784 variants (88.9%) classified as functionally neutral using the gamma GLM were similarly classified using log2 normalized fold change (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two classification methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: 1586 of 1784 variants (88.9%) classified as functionally neutral using the gamma GLM were similarly classified using log2 normalized fold change.
source: Notably, 517 of 525 variants (98.5%) classified as functionally deleterious and 1586 of 1784 variants (88.9%) classified as functionally neutral using the gamma GLM were similarly classified using log2 normalized fold change (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two classification methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Use of in silico models for clinical variant interpretation, including those utilizing machine learning, may be premature.
source: Given that reclassification of VUSs in hereditary cancer genes into inappropriate strata has significant implications for patients, use of in silico models for clinical variant interpretation, including those utilizing machine learning, may be premature.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the performance data of in silico models and speculation about clinical implications.

claim: Current ACMG guidelines include in silico predictions of variant effect as supporting evidence of pathogenicity or benign impact.
source: Ultimately, our data support current ACMG guidelines that include in silico predictions of variant effect as supporting evidence of pathogenicity or benign impact.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study results and knowledge of ACMG guidelines.

claim: ACMG guidelines include presence of a missense variant at a residue with a previously reported pathogenic variant as moderate evidence of pathogenicity.
source: ACMG guidelines include presence of a missense variant at a residue with a previously reported pathogenic variant as moderate evidence of pathogenicity.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of ACMG variant interpretation guidelines.

claim: The presence of a pathogenic missense variant at a residue should be used with caution when classifying other missense variants at the same residue, at least for CDKN2A.
source: Suggesting, at least for CDKN2A, that the presence of a pathogenic missense variant at a residue should be used with caution when classifying other missense variants at the same residue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the finding that no CDKN2A residue was completely intolerant of amino acid changes.

claim: The functional assay may not encompass all cellular functions of CDKN2A.
source: Our assay may not encompass all cellular functions of CDKN2A and an alternative assay of a specific CDKN2A function, such as CDK4 binding, may result in different variant functional classifications.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential limitations of the assay.

claim: An alternative assay of a specific CDKN2A function, such as CDK4 binding, may result in different variant functional classifications.
source: Our assay may not encompass all cellular functions of CDKN2A and an alternative assay of a specific CDKN2A function, such as CDK4 binding, may result in different variant functional classifications.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential alternative assay approaches.

claim: CDKN2A variants may have different effects if alternative cell lines are used for the functional assay.
source: Furthermore, CDKN2A variants may have different effects if alternative cell lines are used for the functional assay.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential cell line-specific effects.

claim: Cell-specific effects appear to be limited based on previous studies.
source: However, cell-specific effects appear to be limited. In our previous study, we characterized 29 CDKN2A VUSs in three PDAC cell lines, using cell proliferation and cell cycle assays, and found agreement between all functional classifications (Kimura et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Functionally deleterious effects were enriched among somatic missense mutations compared to all CDKN2A missense variants.
source: Moreover, we found that functionally deleterious effects were enriched among somatic missense mutations, and depleted in missense VUSs in gnomAD, compared to all CDKN2A missense variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of functional classifications across different variant datasets.

claim: Functionally deleterious effects were depleted in missense VUSs in gnomAD compared to all CDKN2A missense variants.
source: Moreover, we found that functionally deleterious effects were enriched among somatic missense mutations, and depleted in missense VUSs in gnomAD, compared to all CDKN2A missense variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of functional classifications across different variant datasets.
